title: Vandetanib: RET-positive medullary thyroid cancer
indication_text: RET mutation positive, unresectable locally advanced or metastatic medullary thyroid cancer.
purpose: This treatment aims to slow cancer growth and help control symptoms. Your team explains the expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for your situation.
schedule_summary: Vandetanib 300 mg once daily, continuously, until progression or unacceptable side effects.
administration_text: Take at the same time daily, with or without food. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless less than 12 hours remain before the next dose; then skip it. Never double a dose. If swallowing is difficult, disperse the whole tablet without crushing in half a glass of still drinking water, stir for about 10 minutes and drink immediately; rinse the glass with another half-glass and drink. Use no other liquid. Pharmacy must teach feeding-tube administration if needed.
monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney and liver tests at weeks 1, 3, 6 and 12. ECG, potassium, calcium, magnesium and thyroid-stimulating hormone at weeks 1, 3, 6 and 12, then every 3 months for at least a year. Repeat this schedule after a QT-related reduction or interruption longer than 2 weeks. Continue checks after stopping when clinically indicated; monitor blood pressure.

agents.name: Vandetanib
agents.mechanism: Blocks RET and other growth signals
agents.explanation: Vandetanib blocks RET and other enzymes involved in cancer growth and blood-vessel development. It can also change the heart’s electrical recovery, making ECG and blood-salt monitoring essential.
agents.watch: Carry the manufacturer’s patient alert card and receive one with every prescription. Report fainting or palpitations urgently. Check every new medicine for heart-rhythm interactions. Diarrhoea can disturb blood salts and increase rhythm risk. Protect skin from sunlight.
risks: Heart-rhythm disturbance (QT prolongation and torsades de pointes), fainting
Diarrhoea, nausea, reduced appetite and fatigue
Rash, sun sensitivity and rare severe blistering skin reactions
High blood pressure, bleeding and thyroid hormone changes
Rare lung inflammation and neurological syndrome with confusion or seizures
Pregnancy and breastfeeding risks; adverse effects may persist after stopping

anatomy: Balance activity and rest. Sudden confusion, seizure, severe headache or a change in vision needs urgent help.
Report ulcers, pain, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing or weight loss early. Ask for oral care, dietetic and swallowing support.
Follow prescribed heart and blood-pressure checks. Chest pain, fainting, palpitations or new breathlessness needs urgent advice.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt review; serious causes include infection or lung injury.
Use prescribed support. Report persistent diarrhoea or vomiting, inability to drink, blood or severe abdominal pain.
Report reduced urine, swelling or poor fluid intake; keep blood and urine tests.
Report painful palms or soles, rash or blistering early. Severe spreading rash or mouth/eye involvement needs urgent review.
Discuss fertility preservation, contraception, pregnancy and breastfeeding before starting.

evidence.title: What the evidence can tell you
evidence.intro: Research supports a treatment discussion; it cannot predict one person’s outcome.
evidence.population: RET mutation positive, unresectable locally advanced or metastatic medullary thyroid cancer.
evidence.comparison: Placebo in the cited randomised trial
evidence.interpretation: In the randomised placebo-controlled ZETA study, progression-free survival favoured vandetanib (hazard ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.31–0.69). The vandetanib median had not been reached: 30.5 months was a statistical prediction, compared with an observed placebo median of 19.3 months. These values do not predict individual survival. Current RET-positive eligibility must be checked separately from the original study population.
limitations: Trial populations and schedules differ; comparisons across separate trials are unreliable.
An improvement in progression-free survival is not automatically an overall-survival benefit.
